extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and practitioners of political theory and public opinion
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of democracy and public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains the political-theory premises and practical conditions that the author argues are required for functioning democracy and meaningful public opinion (e.g., limits of citizens' knowledge, self-contained communities, checks and balances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Range of attention / limits of political knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: "the attention available would have to be confined to matters close at hand"; citizens can only have reliable political judgment about what lies within their direct and certain knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's maxim: 'If the citizens of a state are to judge and distribute offices according to merit, then they must know each other's characters.' The text emphasizes that political science historically assumed limited range of attention and that this constrains which political questions can be judged spontaneously by ordinary citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that citizens know relevant facts
rubrics_metrics.description: For popular judgment to be sound, citizens must possess the facts necessary for judging public affairs; without such knowledge, elections and decisions "will go wrong."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book argues this applies to every school of political thought and poses special difficulties for democrats with large electorates; implication: reliable public opinion presumes accessible, shared factual knowledge among decision-makers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneous public opinion assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Early democrats assumed that "public opinion did not come forth spontaneously" was inconceivable — they assumed the voice of the people would arise naturally and be a trustworthy guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assumption led democrats not to consider how to inform voters; critics pointed out fallibility, susceptibility to being fooled, and unequal fitness to govern. The text treats this assumption as a central premise that can be questioned once mechanisms of information exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-contained community / self-sufficiency as condition for democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy functions best in an environment "confined within the range of the ruler's direct and certain knowledge" — small, simple, self-governing communities (e.g., rural townships) where affairs are familiar and manageable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jeffersonian ideal of small landowning farmers exemplifies this. The democratic stereotype requires fencing off ideal communities from complex external interactions (manufacture, foreign commerce, big cities) to preserve spontaneous self-government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omnicompetent citizen ideal and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic doctrine held that "one man was as competent as the next to manage these simple and self-contained affairs" — the 'omnicompetent citizen'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is practically true in small townships (rotation in office, jacks-of-all-trades) but breaks down when applied universally to a complex, interconnected civilization; universal application produces serious problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common information and shared pictures of the world
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion relies on shared stereotyped images of the outside world formed by parents, teachers, church, pamphlets, and weak newspapers; when these are the chief sources, opinions are based on casual fancy rather than objective reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that modern institutions (newspapers, measurement, record, quantitative analysis) can change this by bringing the unseen world into the field of judgment, but historically there was little reliable reporting to ground public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of measurement, record, and analysis for extending judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventions of measurement, record, quantitative and comparative analysis, and psychological analysis are key to 'bringing the unseen world into the field of judgment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although these instruments are imperfect and often used badly, their existence makes it feasible for amateurs to form valuable judgments about distant and complex events; their growth undermines the older premises that limited democratic judgment to local matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security and stability as prerequisites for democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy requires as little disturbance as possible of the premise of a self-contained community; insecurity and crises, which demand quick decisions by a few, are seen as incompatible with democratic spontaneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues democracies prefer security/isolation to avoid surprises that force centralized rapid action; democratic wars historically framed as defensive or for pacifist aims due to this constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic legalism and reliance on fixed principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Because communities often had to 'live on their capital' of received wisdom, Americans turned to legalism — a tested body of rules and fixed principles — to achieve self-sufficiency in public life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This static theorism allowed communities to avoid re-earning truths by experience, but also meant public opinions were constructed from a few stereotyped images and codes rather than fresh empirical inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federalist remedy: checks and balances to neutralize local opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: To offset the problem of many self-centered communities acting at cross-purposes, the Constitution's checks and balances were designed so that 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition' and to 'enable the government to control the governed' while obliging it 'to control itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a practical mechanism to substitute institutional restraint for the absent coordination of shared information across communities; it is a deliberate limit on the sphere of popular rule, relying on balancing special interests rather than assuming a common informed citizenry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical politics: selection of governing classes and attachment through interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The framers deliberately sought to attract men whose passions could be attached to national interest (the gentry, public creditors, manufacturers, shippers, and traders) to secure effective governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton used fiscal and institutional measures to bind provincial notables to the new government; the constitution thus used class alignments and patronage to make union feasible in the absence of a coordinated popular information system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat about cynical realism (Machiavelli) regarding subjective judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Machiavelli observed that 'men judge generally more by the eye than by the hand' — people's judgments are subjective and based on appearances, which leads to perpetual strife among self-centered groups whose private visions conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This realist diagnosis implies that without means to correct subjective visions (through reporting, measurement, or institutions), political life will be dominated by competition among partial, self-centered perceptions; it underpins arguments for institutional checks or for limiting the domain of popular decision-making.
